rewrites.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal — one of few nations in the region never to criminalise it: a 1993 penal code decree omits same-sex offences and a 2014 domestic-violence law protects victims regardless of sexual orientation. No legal gender recognition, no trans framework and no partnership recognition exist, and there is no anti-discrimination protection, so no document or screening pathway for trans travelers is documented.

Enforcement and practical safety dominate: chronic instability (a 2012 coup), a weak national apparatus, documented impunity for security-force abuse (arbitrary killings, torture), documented social hostility and stigma, some violence cases in 2018, no visible LGBT scene, and a poor 34/100 ('Caution') travel-safety score, with no mob-lynching pattern reported for a neighbouring nation.
rewrites.tangentialFactors:
Comparisons with the region colour the visit: the nation is one of few in the region never to criminalise same-sex conduct, a small minority finds homosexual behaviour morally acceptable — unusually moderate for the region — and it lacks the mob-lynching pattern reported for a neighbouring nation, so these comparisons temper worst-case expectations.

The international setting is adjacent but non-binding: the nation signed the 2008 UN statement on sexual orientation and gender identity, and secondary overview sources note legal challenges in the area, signalling an unsettled rather than settled policy space. The security reporting used here (2011–2012) comes from foreign-government sources, covers a period of coups and predates the current decade.
rewrites.localsOnly: Resident-facing: only married heterosexual couples qualify for larger government housing; a small share (9%) of residents considers homosexual behaviour morally acceptable; no visible LGBT scene; female genital mutilation is documented in the 2011 security report; the 2014 domestic-violence law protects resident victims regardless of sexual orientation.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: Passport marker and border-screening treatment for trans travelers is not documented in any source; with no legal gender recognition, no procedure for aligning identity documents is identified. Security reporting dates to 2011–2012, secondary overview pages are derived from an open encyclopaedia, and sources focus on LGB matters rather than trans-specific experiences, so trans-specific local data remains unverifiable.

Blind mirrors substitution-only per rules 7/7e; the 9% survey figure and the 34/100 score are generalised in blind texts.
